head.meta_description: Catering trends 2026 in Dubai: what is actually changing in private and event dining, based on myCHEF
head.h1: Dubai Food Trends Report 2026: Catering Trends — Real Prices and Timings

opening_paragraph: The catering trends 2026 that matter in Dubai are less about novelty ingredients and more about format, dietary range and provenance. Below is what we at myCHEF see changing in our own bookings, stated as our observation instead of as market data, alongside the fixed points that have not moved: seasonality, food-safety obligations and a price floor of around AED 700 per person.

add_block.new_heading: Trend 1: dietary range as the default, not the exception
new_paragraphs: The clearest change over recent seasons is that dietary requirements are now a planning input instead of a late accommodation. A typical Dubai guest list spans halal as standard, plus vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, dairy-free and nut-free needs, and increasingly low-sugar or low-carb preferences alongside them. Hosts now ask for this at the briefing stage instead of forwarding a list a week out.

The practical effect on menu design is significant. The approach that works is a menu where the plant-based and allergen-aware dishes are designed to be good in their own right and served to the whole table, instead of a separate plate carried out apologetically. It also changes timing: dietary covers planned into the count are plated in the same service wave, so those guests are not eating ten minutes after the table.

add_block.new_heading: Trend 2: interactive formats over static buffets
new_paragraphs: Live stations, chef's tables and food built in front of guests keep gaining ground on the traditional buffet at mid-size events. The reason is partly that a station is an experience and photographs well, and partly practical: stations split a queue, keep food hot and give the room a focal point. A single buffet line for a hundred people creates a bottleneck; three stations do not.

For hosts, the trade-off is cost and space. Each station needs a chef, so the labour line rises, and stations need floor area that a buffet against a wall does not. Some ideas that work well in Dubai villas and venues: a grill or shawarma station outdoors in the cooler months, a pasta or wok pan indoors, and a dessert station as a second focal point later in the evening. Our live cooking stations page covers the formats.

add_block.new_heading: Trend 3: provenance questions, and shorter menus done properly
new_paragraphs: Guests and hosts increasingly ask where things come from, and hosts ask more pointed questions about the chef than about the dish list. That is a healthy shift. Alongside it we see menus getting shorter: four well-executed courses instead of seven, and a tighter canape list served generously instead of a long list served thinly.

This is a good trend for the food. A shorter menu concentrates the kitchen's attention, reduces waste and usually eats better. It is also more economical, which matters when the same budget has to stretch across styling, staffing and rentals. If you are planning for 2026, the useful tip is to spend the budget on fewer, better dishes and on the people cooking them.

add_block.new_heading: How the 2026 trends land by occasion
new_paragraphs: The same shifts show up differently depending on what you are hosting.

Wedding catering trends 2026. A grazing table through the welcome, one live station at the reception, and a shorter seated menu executed properly instead of a long one executed thinly. Dietary covers are collected with the RSVPs and plated in the same wave as everyone else. Wedding dates sit inside the November-to-March window, so they commit earlier than anything else in the calendar — 7 to 14 days is the working lead time for the catering itself, but the date goes long before that.

Corporate catering trends 2026. The working lunch has separated from the event dinner, and companies now buy them as two different things. Volume formats — working lunch, drop-off, buffet — start from AED 90 per person, while a staffed dinner with a chef cooking on site sits in the AED 700–950 band. The first is ordered more often and at shorter notice; the second is ordered more deliberately, for fewer occasions.

Small catering trends 2026. Small events are the fastest-changing part of our book. A sixteen-guest dinner now gets what a hundred-guest event used to get: a designed menu, a live element, a chef in the room. Volume formats need 10 guests and a buffet needs 20, but a private chef cooking plated has no minimum headcount, so a small table is not priced out of the good version of the evening.

Summer. Food trends for summer 2026 are set by the heat, not by fashion. Service moves indoors or after sunset, chilled mezze and raw seafood displace slow-roasted centrepieces, and anything on a grill happens on a shaded terrace or not at all. Summer is also when dates are easiest to get and menus are easiest to change.
Where 2026 sits next to 2025

Very little here is new against 2025, and that is the useful part. Every trend on this page was visible in 2025 and has since become normal: dietary planning moved from a request to a default, live stations moved from a feature to an expectation, menus kept getting shorter. What changed year on year is the size of each shift, not its direction. Anyone selling a reinvention of catering between one year and the next is selling copy.
The ten-year view

Reading food trends by year makes each one look larger than it is. Set against the last 10 years — myCHEF is part of Global Catering, which has been operating in this market since 2015 — three things have changed, and they changed slowly. Dietary requirements went from an exception handled at the door to a design input taken at the brief. Cooking moved out of the back kitchen and into the room. And hosts started asking who the chef is before they ask what is on the menu. Most of what appears in a trends list is seasoning on those three.
The current picture in the catering industry

Put together, the current trends in the catering industry as myCHEF sees them are: dietary range as a default, live formats over static ones, provenance questions about the chef, shorter menus, vegetable-led and fire-cooked food, plainer plating, and drinks planned as carefully as the food. That is the whole list. It is short because everything we cannot see from our own bookings has been left off it.

new_paragraphs: Three fixed points still shape every Dubai event. Seasonality: the outdoor window runs November to March, when days average around 27°C and nights fall to about 19°C ( Weather and Climate ), and those months carry weddings, galas and the conference calendar at once. Venue pressure is rising instead of easing — the Dubai World Trade Centre opens a new Dubai Exhibition Centre in 2026 — so peak dates commit early.

Food safety is the second fixed point. Licensed caterers work to the Dubai Municipality Food Code, covering transport and delivery vehicles as well as handling, with mandatory structured staff training. The Dubai Municipality Food Safety Department monitors food establishments and investigates food-borne illness, so compliance is checked in practice. The third is price: catering still starts from around AED 700 per person, with tasting formats from about AED 1,400 and event minimums of AED 2,400 or AED 3,600 for larger builds. Trends change the menu; they have not moved the floor. Every quote carries 5% VAT.

new_paragraphs: What are the main catering trends in Dubai for 2026?

Dietary range treated as standard planning instead of a special request, interactive live formats displacing static buffets at mid-size events, more questions about provenance, and shorter menus executed properly.
Is this report based on market research?
No. It describes patterns myCHEF observes in its own Dubai bookings. It is first-party observation and not a market study, and no percentages are attached because that would mean inventing figures.
Have catering prices changed for 2026?

The floor has not moved. Catering still starts from around AED 700 per person, tasting formats from about AED 1,400, and larger events carry minimums of AED 2,400 or AED 3,600. All quotes carry 5% VAT.
Are buffets going away?
Not entirely, but live stations keep taking share at mid-size events because they split queues, keep food hot and give the room a focal point. Stations cost more in labour and need more floor space.
How should I handle dietary requirements in 2026?

Collect them with the RSVPs and treat them as a design input. The approach that works is plant-based and allergen-aware dishes good enough for the whole table, plated in the same service wave as the rest of the table.
When is peak season for Dubai events?
November to March, when days average around 27°C and nights about 19°C. Weddings, galas and the conference calendar overlap in those months, so popular dates commit early.
What is the most useful planning change for 2026?
Spend on fewer, better dishes and on the people cooking them. A shorter menu concentrates the kitchen, reduces waste and usually eats better than a long one.
What are the big food trends for 2026?

At the food level: vegetables at the centre of a dish instead of at the side, charcoal and open-fire cooking, regional specificity in place of a broad cuisine label, lighter fruit-led desserts, and pickled or fermented elements used as acid against rich plates. These are shifts in emphasis, not new ingredients.
What are the food design trends in 2026?

Plainer plating with colour from the ingredient instead of from garnish, portions sized to be finished, sharing formats such as grazing tables and carved centrepieces, and canapés built as one filling on one base to be eaten in a single bite.
What are the wedding catering trends for 2026?

A grazing table through the welcome, one live station at the reception, and a shorter seated menu executed properly. Dietary covers are collected with the RSVPs and served in the same wave as everyone else. Peak wedding dates fall between November and March and commit earliest.
How is 2026 different from 2025?

In direction, it is not. Every trend here was visible in 2025 and has since become normal rather than notable: dietary planning as a default, live stations as an expectation, menus getting shorter. What changed year on year is the size of each shift.
